citation: Dolfen, Einav, Klenow, Klopack, Levin, Levin, Best. Assessing the Gains from E-Commerce. NBER WP 25610 (Feb 2019); AEJ: Macroeconomics 15(1):342-370 (2023). (This is the Einav/Klenow paper and the Dolfen paper - one paper.)
data: Visa credit/debit transactions 2007-2017 (avg 380M cards, 35.9B transactions, $1.93T/yr); card-present vs card-not-present flag
finding: Online share of Visa spending in NAICS category rose 2007 -> 2017 (Table 2): electronics 42->51%, furniture 35->43%, clothing 22->37%, general merchandise 8->15%, food 5->6%, nonstore retailers 90->96%. Online = ~5% of all consumption 2007 -> ~8% 2017 (retail-only ~3.5% -> ~5%).
key_numbers: Convenience gain <=0.4% of consumption; most gain is variety (switching to online-only merchants). Within-merchant: moving 10 -> 20 miles from nearest store raises online share of purchases ~3 pts (Table/Sec 4). Elasticity of substitution online vs offline merchants 4.3 overall; 3.4 electronics to 7.7 building materials (Table 9).
categories_covered: furniture, electronics, clothing, sporting/hobby/books, misc, general merchandise, food (Table 2, Table 3, Table 9)
caveats: WP version, not the published AEJ text. Share is of Visa card spend, scaled to consumption; assumes Visa online share representative. Does not measure trips or floor space; the 'trip' cost is a distance proxy.

citation: Relihan, L.E. Is online retail killing coffee shops? Estimating the winners and losers of online retail using customer transaction microdata. CEP Discussion Paper 1836 (Mar 2022).
data: JPMorgan Chase Institute de-identified daily card transactions, 69M customers Oct 2012-May 2017; panel of ~7.7M; early adopters of online grocery platforms vs matched non-users
data_access: JPMCI data restricted (data-use agreement); paper public
finding: Early online-grocery adopters cut grocery-store trips by 0.5 days/month (6.8 -> 6.3, -7.4%) but spend 12.3% more on local ground transport and take more trips to coffee shops (+1.3 days/yr), leisure, personal care, restaurants (+2.3), and pharmacies (+0.9). No increase in trips for clothing, general goods, home goods.
substitution_vs_complementarity: partial substitution for the replaced store (grocery); complementarity for time-intensive services; no new goods trips
key_numbers: Counterfactual: platform adoption 1.7% -> 9.2% would cut mean zip-code grocery trip frequency 2.0% and raise coffee-shop frequency 3.4%.
caveats: Trip = card-transaction day, so trips without card payment are invisible; early adopters not representative; groceries only.

citation: Chava, Oettl, Singh, Zeng. Creative Destruction? Impact of E-Commerce on the Retail Sector. NBER WP 30077 (May 2022); Management Science 70(4):2168-2187 (2024).
data: Staggered rollout of a major e-commerce firm's fulfillment centers (firm not named in the text: first center 1997, over 90 by end-2016, which matches Amazon; Amazon appears only in cited news URLs and references) vs payroll data for 2.6M retail workers and data on 3.2M stores
data_access: Payroll and store data are commercial/restricted; paper public
verification_status: OPENED (NBER full text searched for categories and firm name, saved data/raw/interp_spend/papers/chava_nber_w30077.pdf)
finding: A new fulfillment center lowers sales at proximate stores by 4% (employment -2.1%); store exit probability rises ~3 pts, entry falls; retail sector loses 938 jobs per county-quarter.
key_numbers: Sales -4% and employment -2.1% at stores near a fulfillment center; classified retail 3-digit NAICS 442, 444, 448, 451 etc. in the exposure definition.
categories_covered: NAICS 442, 444, 448, 451 and others (retail categories that compete with the catalog)
caveats: Effect on stores near a center, not total spend shifted; category breakdown not used for the headline; counts store exits, not floor space.

citation: Pozzi, A. The effect of Internet distribution on brick-and-mortar sales. RAND Journal of Economics 44(3):569-583 (2013); Oct 2012 working paper.
data: Household scanner data (almost 10,000 households) from one large supermarket chain that added online shopping
data_access: Chain data restricted (not Nielsen Homescan); WP public
finding: Online grocery sales are mostly incremental: each $1 online crowds out less than 40 cents of the chain's own store spend (WP abstract; a search snippet of another version says 45 cents - published figure not verified). Store revenues up 13% in the zip code once the service launches.
substitution_vs_complementarity: mostly complementary for the retailer; crowd-out low and shrinks with distance from stores
key_numbers: Crowd-out <$0.40 per $1 online; +13% zip-level chain revenue.
caveats: One chain; share-stealing from rivals is part of the 'incremental' revenue, so it is not net household-level complementarity.

citation: Forman, Ghose, Goldfarb. Competition between local and electronic markets: how the benefit of buying online depends on where you live. Management Science 55(1):47-57.
data: Amazon book sales ranks for 1,497 US locations, ~10 months to Jan 2006; local store openings (Barnes & Noble, Borders, Wal-Mart, Target)
data_access: Public rank data scraped by authors; paper public
finding: Online book purchasing falls when a physical store opens nearby: online and local stores are substitutes at the margin; offline entry also lowers sensitivity to online price discounts.

citation: Zhou, Y. and Wang, X. Explore the relationship between online shopping and shopping trips: an analysis with the 2009 NHTS data. Transportation Research Part A 70:1-9.
data: 2009 National Household Travel Survey (public use), structural equation model
finding: Online shopping increases the number of shopping trips (complementarity); shopping trips lower online-shopping propensity (store shopping substitutes for online).
caveats: Cross-section, self-reported online shopping on a points scale; causality is not identified.

citation: Atlanta Fed Diary of Consumer Payment Choice 2020-2025 public microdata (this build); earlier years via Boston Fed
data: 3-day payment diary, ~3,000-5,000 US consumers/yr, October of each year
finding: Remote (online, mail, phone) share of purchases about 20% 2020-2022 (double 2019 per Atlanta Fed text) and 24% of purchases by number in 2025 (report text). Category cut is coarse: merchant code 5 lumps general merchandise, department, other stores AND online shopping.
caveats: Payments, not trips; no category detail within stores; remote includes bills-like prepayments only for purchases.

citation: McGuckin and Fucci. Summary of Travel Trends: 2017 NHTS, Table 10a
finding: Shopping-and-errand person trips per person per year: 668 (1995), 608 (2001), 588 (2009), 473 (2017). Report attributes part of the drop to online shopping but does not measure it and warns about method changes.

citation: NielsenIQ Consumer Panel (Homescan) via Kilts Center, University of Chicago
data: ~40-60k US households scanning UPC purchases incl. online retailers
finding: No public category-level online share found. A search-result summary of an AEA working paper says the panel shows a growing online share over time, and a Fed discussion deck notes weak compliance for frequent small online purchases and ~4.9% of consumption coverage (Baker and Kueng figure).
caveats: Do not cite these as measured shares.

citation: Numerator Total Commerce Panel / OmniPanel (receipt-based, ~200,000 households per company statements)
data: Receipt capture across store and online
finding: Company survey report 'State of Commerce 2026' (survey of 2,000+ consumers, not the panel) says online share of 1-2 item baskets rose from 16% to 32% and of stock-up baskets from 3% to 12% since 2019. Not verified against the report.

citation: Morduch and Schneider. The Financial Diaries (Princeton UP 2017); US Financial Diaries 2012-13
data: 235 households in 4 communities, every financial transaction for a year
data_access: Public summaries; household data on request
finding: Not usable here: tiny, non-representative, 2012-13 only, built for income volatility and borrowing. Search results show no channel (online vs store) field and no category-level spending breakdown.
caveats: Say 'no evidence of a channel field', not 'confirmed absent'.

citation: BLS Division of CE Surveys, Lee and Abdirizak, AAPOR 2019 slides
data: CE Interview final wave Jul 2017-Mar 2018, 1,100 test households (4,517 completed interviews)
data_access: Test only; not a public time series
finding: A 'Purchase mode: online or in-person' question was tested in 10 CE Interview sections, along with store name and location. Only 224 households answered the purchase-mode question. No findings on online share in the deck.
caveats: Production CE public-use files: no outlet or online variable found (see notes).
